title: The vine (John 15:1–8)
hookLine: abide in me; without me you can do nothing

lines: A CUT ROSE, ON A CLOCK.
cards: Cut a rose for a vase and it looks perfect for a day or two. Same color, same petals, same smell as the one still on the bush. But it's already on a clock.
It has everything except a connection. Nothing is flowing into it anymore. At the end of chapter fourteen Jesus says, arise, let us go hence.
Some readers picture them leaving the supper room and walking out into the dark. John doesn't say where they are. What comes next is a vine.

teach.h: ANOTHER I AM: THE TRUE VINE.
teach.b: It's another of John's I am sayings, and the Douay-Rheims begins: "I am the true vine; and my Father is the husbandman." Husbandman is the old word for farmer, the one who tends the vines.
In the Hebrew scriptures, Israel itself is pictured as God's vine, planted and cared for. Jesus takes the picture personally.
Then the key verse: "I am the vine; you the branches: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same beareth much fruit: for without me you can do nothing." The word to hold is abide.

In Greek it's menō, to stay, remain, live somewhere, and it shows up again and again in these few verses. A branch doesn't produce fruit by straining or trying harder. It stays attached, and the sap does the work.
There's a hard note too: the farmer prunes. Every branch that bears fruit, he cuts back, so it bears more.

Anyone who's watched a grapevine pruned in winter knows how brutal it looks, bare stubs where there were long canes, and how much fruit comes that summer. Catholics hear the vine in two places especially.
One is the Eucharist, the fruit of the vine on the altar. The other is the ordinary day.
Some saints recommended very short prayers through the day, sometimes called aspirations: a name or a single line, said while washing dishes or waiting at a light, like Jesus, Mary, Joseph.
Not a long prayer. Just staying connected.

how: Many Catholics pray short aspirations through the day, a name or a single line such as "Jesus, Mary, Joseph," alongside longer prayer at Mass and at home.

the world, where good and bad grow together

s: a branch bears fruit by trying harder
it bears fruit by staying attached: he that abideth in me.
in this passage the farmer cuts back the fruitful branches too
so that they bear more fruit.

games.q: you're a branch on a grapevine and you want to bear fruit. what does Jesus say you do?
o: grow as fast as you can.
games.why: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same beareth much fruit: for without me you can do nothing.

practice: Notice where your body is held: feet on the floor, back against the chair, hands resting, and let your weight settle there. Don't try to do anything; just remain, and when your mind wanders, come back to those points of contact.
If you pray, hold one short line from the Gospel, abide in me; if you don't, simply stay where you are.

wordCard.voice: The vine. Jesus is the vine and his followers the branches: whoever abides in him bears much fruit. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: I abide, stay, remain. It runs all through John 15.
